newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Siemens steps up pace of reorganisation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Siemens steps up pace of reorganisation.

text.p: BONN, March 11 (Rueter) - German electronics and engineering titan Siemens AG on Tuesday showed further signs of speeding up its reorganisation and divestment in an effort to put profit back on a growth path.

The company's transportation systems unit (VT) forecast a larger than expected 1996-97 loss of 60 million to 100 million marks ($35.2 million-$56.9 million) and said it would out-source some manufacturing and cut about 800 jobs in Germany.
Meanwhile, Siemens's defence electronics unit confirmed it had hired U.S. investment bank Morgan Stanley to help to find a buyer or possible joint venture partner for the business.
"I do sense a bit of acceleration, a slight hastening of the process," said Peter Roe, a Banque Paribas analyst in London. "These things they are doing should be well received by the markets."
Siemens has come under pressure to boost profitability since a November warning that it expected no profit improvement in 1996-97, which ends September 30.

In January the company said it would sell off businesses with turnover of more than three billion marks this year, but shareholders still sharply criticised Siemens management at the annual general meeting last month.

The transport unit, which produces mass transit systems and locomotives, said it had budgeted for a loss of 80 million marks, due to a 68 million mark restructuring charge and more than 100 million marks in costs related to outstanding orders.
Still, price competition would keep sales and orders stable at the 1995-96 levels of 4.3 billion marks and 6.5 billion marks, respectively.
The size of this year's expected loss surprised analysts, who had predicted a setback for VT of about 50 million marks.
"They had some bad orders but seemed to be working through them, so this is disappointing," Roe said.

To boost profit, the unit planned to spin off production of overhead lines and power supplies in a management buyout, to transfer another non-rail activity to Siemens' power transmission unit and to cut its headquarter staff 30 percent.
The unit would also increase cooperation with competitors to break into new markets, unit head Wolfram Martinsen said at a news conference in Vienna.

Siemens would market rail systems with General Motors Corp.'s locomotive unit, and building mass transit systems in two Chinese cities with ADtranz, he said. With France's GEC Alsthom, the unit would market their high-speed train technology together.
"We are making the tough decisions in order to thrive in the future," Martinsen said.

A small profit in 1997/98 was possible, and the group expected profitability to improve to a five percent return on sales by 2000, although that figure was well below the group goal of 15 percent return on sales.

Analysts were sceptical. "This is a super-competitive industry and there's not a lot of growth," said one Frankfurt analyst who did not want to be identified. "Europe has done a lot of modernising, and in eastern Europe financing is a question for big projects."

The transport reorganisation came as Siemens seemed to be nearing a sale of its defence electronics business, which is centred on its Siemens Plessey unit in Great Britain. Two weeks ago Siemens Plessey told employees it sought a partner for a joint venture.
On Tuesday, the electronics group confirmed it had hired Morgan Stanely, but would not confirm a newspaper report that it was now only seeking a sell off.
